cards.enhancedTitle: Why networks exist: origins and business need
cards.addedExplanation: [Added — not owner's text] Networks did not start with computers. They started with people signalling to each other, then with mechanical signals, then with the telegraph — and business needed them because a deal is only as fast as the information behind it. That need is why organisations, rules and coordination appear before any device in this sequence.
cards.enhancedDiagram: [Added diagram — redraw, different style from the original] A horizontal timeline: Human to human, then Mechanical signals, then Electronic telegraph, then DARPA 1960, with a second lane underneath: Business need (speed of trade) leading to Organisation, then Regulation and coordination. [Audit 2026-10-29: arrows in batch1-notes.md are now labelled by kind; see diagramArrowKinds.]
originalKeyPoints: Before agencies of networks: human to human (oral language, signals, written text), then mechanical-signaling systems (fire beacons, drums), then electronic — telegraph.
(1960) DARPA, US Defense Agency network, as written on the page.
Business = exchange of information; speed of business = trading; speed of trading = exchange of information.

Business organisation: ownership, board, investors, executive team, C-suite, middle management, departments — under five rule layers: tech standards, governance and coordination, national and international regulation, privacy and security, market rules.
Regulation, monopolies, coordination (IETF), trust and security, government-funded physical network and infrastructure projects.
cards.title: Why networks exist: origins and business need

cards.enhancedTitle: Naming, addressing and regulation: directory to DNS
cards.addedExplanation: [Added — not owner's text] Before DNS, the directory was a telephone book run by government. The internet kept the directory idea but changed who runs it and how it scales: names are delegated hierarchically, addresses are allocated in blocks by region, and both are wrapped in regulation and privacy rules. That is why naming and regulation belong in one card, not in separate ones.
cards.enhancedDiagram: [Added diagram — redraw, different style from the original] Left to right: Telephone directory, then DNS in the centre, then ICANN at the top, RIRs (ARIN / RIPE / APNIC) below it, then ISP, then user. A regulator lane underneath: FCC / TRAI, with standards bodies IETF / IEEE / 3GPP beside it. [Audit 2026-10-29: arrows in batch1-notes.md are now labelled by kind; see diagramArrowKinds.]
originalKeyPoints: Market rules: antitrust, net neutrality, as written on the page.
Government telephone directory, with options: writing up, directory management (ICANN, RIR), keypad / switchboard controls, privacy lock (data and communication, MAC plus IP).
Replace phone directory with DNS.
ICANN: non-profit, multi-stakeholder, domain (company names), hierarchical, country codes, area codes, TLDs, IP ranges.
RIRs: ARIN, RIPE, APNIC — IP blocks allocation. IP as identity. DNSSEC, registration, owner, trust, key and security.
Telecom regulation: IETF, IEEE, 3GPP standards; FCC, TRAI; DNS owners, TLD, shareholders, board, executives.
FCC as telecom regulator (1934 as written on the page) over radio, TV, satellite, wireline, wireless, broadband and spectrum, through telecom companies to spectrum decisions.
cards.title: Naming, addressing and regulation: directory to DNS
cards.verticalPosition: After the business frame: how things are named, addressed and regulated.

cards.enhancedTitle: Hardware supply and the NIC endpoint
cards.addedExplanation: [Added — not owner's text] Silicon becomes a chip, a chip becomes a vendor's device, and that device only reaches a customer through an endpoint: the NIC. Selling that endpoint is not just a shipment — it is governed, which is why the NIC chain in the notes keeps returning to government rules and to FCC.
cards.enhancedDiagram: [Added diagram — redraw, different style from the original] Top to bottom: Silicon, then Intel / Broadcom / Nvidia, then Cloud / OEMs / Telco-ISP / Government labs, with the NIC as the endpoint box at the bottom, connected by PCI to the device. [Audit 2026-10-29: arrows in batch1-notes.md are now labelled by kind; see diagramArrowKinds.]
originalKeyPoints: Silicon product, government device, business — to Intel, Broadcom, Nvidia as supplier, hardware.
End customers: cloud, OEMs, telco / ISP, research by government (DRDO / NASA), C-suite, IoT.
NIC to PCI, visible via interface; NIC contains; sell to customers who follow government rules; PCI device, driver, user tools, workload, OS.
Market vendors Intel / Broadcom / Nvidia supply hardware controlled by software.
Direct buyers: cloud (AWS, GCP), OEMs (Dell, HPE, Lenovo, Cisco), telcos and ISP (AT&T, Verizon, Jio), government labs, assemblers — NIC integrated into devices.
DARPA, TCP/IP, device options, remotes, connections, as written on the page.
cards.title: Hardware supply and the NIC endpoint
cards.verticalPosition: After naming: what physical thing carries those names and addresses.

cards.enhancedTitle: The NIC and kernel stack, plus out-of-band management
cards.addedExplanation: [Added — not owner's text] This card has two lanes that must not be confused. The data lane goes customer, interface, driver, kernel, net device, TCP/IP. The management lane sits beside it: out-of-band to BMC, then CLI, web or API, and it works even when the data lane does not. Learning them as one stack hides the second lane; learning them as two lanes explains why a device can be managed while it is down.
cards.enhancedDiagram: [Added diagram — redraw, different style from the original] Two parallel lanes. Data lane: End customer, Interface, Driver, Kernel stack, Net device, TCP/IP. Management lane, separate and below: OOB, BMC / ILO, then CLI / Web UI / API, then Running config, then Start up to hardware. [Audit 2026-10-29: arrows in batch1-notes.md are now labelled by kind; see diagramArrowKinds.]
originalKeyPoints: End customers, interfaces NIC, drivers implement, kernel stack, net device, TCP/IP.
Computer, storage, hardware, OEM, mounted file system, driven by software for fast trading and communication; switch to transport, router to private IP, NIC to public IP.
Device emulation, core functions, business, ASIC hardware, shared component, libraries (firmware), port to business to network to customer.
Network device, hardware plus software, OEM, network hierarchy, organisation business network, product plus custom.
OOB, BMC / IDC / ILO, sbin / init (power), switch, network switch; options, CLI, sbin to router, IP route, web, Nginx / Apache, DNS book, switch, API / communication / restful / netconf, proc / sys.

Root to OOB, sbin / init to BMC (power), to CLI admin, IP / route / device / config files to start; etc config, startup.config; OOB to BMC / IDRC / ILO to API, web UI, CLI / router, running config, proc / sys, start up to hardware.
cards.title: The NIC and kernel stack, plus out-of-band management
cards.verticalPosition: After supply: how the endpoint actually runs inside a machine.

cards.enhancedTitle: Building, operating and approving a product
cards.addedExplanation: [Added — not owner's text] A product closes the loop: it is built by engineering and operations, tested, sold to customers, bought from vendors who buy silicon, and it cannot enter the market until approval is granted. That approval gate is why this card comes last — it depends on every card before it, from origins to naming to the NIC stack.
cards.enhancedDiagram: [Added diagram — redraw, different style from the original] A loop, left to right and back: C-suite and operations, then Engineering and testing, then Customers, then Vendors, then Silicon, with an FCC approval gate between Vendors / Silicon and the market, marked as a gate, not a step. [Audit 2026-10-29: arrows in batch1-notes.md are now labelled by kind; see diagramArrowKinds.]
originalKeyPoints: Product development, C-suite, admin / deploy service, kernel, middle managers, engineering, operation development, marketing.

Supervisors handle projects, team lead, testing, RF exposure limits, tower siting; employees / workers, technology / engine / customers, switches / routers / network, FCC / customers, vendors, silicon, Intel / Broadcom / Nvidia.
FCC approval: equipment certification (routers / phones must), broadband speed report, as written on the page.
Business organisation and five rule layers, as in Card A, applied here to running a product, not just to owning a business.
Regulation, coordination, trust and security, global phone book, regional / area codes, as in Card A, applied here to market entry.
cards.title: Building, operating and approving a product
cards.verticalPosition: Last: the product that uses all earlier layers, gated by approval.
